items.title: Full Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5 comparison.
items.summary:
Full Opus 5 vs Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 vs Claude Fable 5 comparison.

Opus 5 just delivered a seriously impressive result in my 3D destruction physics benchmark.

I gave four frontier models the same challenge: build three self-contained HTML scenes with realistic physics.

The tasks:

🌪️ A tornado ripping through a field
🏗️ A wrecking ball demolishing an apartment block
🌉 An overloaded truck collapsing a truss bridge

Token usage / cost:
• Opus 5: 55.9K tokens — $1.40
• Fable 5: 55.1K tokens — $2.82
• Kimi K3: 35.7K tokens — $0.55
• GPT-5.6: 20.1K tokens — $0.31

Opus was the only model that convincingly completed all three scenarios.

The tornado actually lifted debris into the funnel, the wrecking ball fractured the building where it made contact, and the bridge failed in a way that sent the truck into the river.

The others struggled in different ways. Fable’s tornado had little to pick up, its building collapsed before impact, and the bridge disintegrated unrealistically. GPT-5.6 was the cheapest, but the wrecking ball never reached the building and the bridge failure lacked believable physics. Kimi K3 landed somewhere in between.

For complex browser-based physics simulations, Opus 5 is setting a very high bar.

items.title: Jim Cramer says Wall Street is fleeing the AI trade and buying these stocks instead
items.summary:
"The stocks just anticipate the ending," he added.

Take Western Digital, the stock hit an all-time closing high of $746 per share on June 18 — at the time, up 333% for the year. Less than six weeks later, the stock is down nearly 40% from its record.

Cramer stressed, however, that investors are not abandoning the market altogether. Instead, they are redeploying capital into companies whose growth depends less on continued AI infrastructure spending. [...] Prime examples are Micron, Western Digital, Seagate, and Sandisk, whose shares soared as shortages of memory used in AI servers gave the companies unprecedented pricing power. After peaking in June, those stocks have tumbled as investors bet those shortages — and the extraordinary profits they created — won't last forever.

"I have been through many boom-bust cycles with these companies," Cramer said. "You have to sell the parabolic moves that these shortages trigger because they always end." [...] CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that Wall Street is taking profits in this year's biggest AI infrastructure winners and rotating into stocks of companies with growth drivers away from the data center.

"You can call it a broadening," the "Mad Money" host said. "Or you can call it fleeing."

Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence data center buildout dominated the market for much of the first half of the year, but many of them have pulled back sharply in recent weeks.

items.title: Sam on being a parent while running OpenAI:

Sam on being a parent while running OpenAI:

“I think I have the best, most interesting job in the world, and it is still a very distant second to having kids.”

“My kids will never grow up in a world where they were smarter than computers.”

“People ask me, now that you have kids, do you care more about AI safety?

The answer is, I didn't need kids for that. I really didn't want to destroy the world before.”

items.title: Sam Altman just said something that should worry you more than excite you:
items.summary:
Sam Altman just said something that should worry you more than excite you: 

"AI is close to creating a genie that can grant any wish."

This is EXACTLY why open-source AI matters - and this was Elon's original thesis when he was at OpenAI. 

Right now, the future of all AI power sits with a handful of companies. 

Think: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta. 

They decide who gets access, at what price, under what rules, and on what timeline.

Open-weight models are the only solution to ensuring this "genius in a bottle" power is in check. 

Ultimately, this is also why it matters that NVIDIA, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and dozens of others just signed a joint letter arguing that we need to pivot towards open-weight AI. 

The most powerful technology in human history should not be something a handful of executives dole out to the world on their own terms.

The bull case for open-source AI is simple: don't let five companies hold all the leverage over everyone else.
https://t.co/zcsXXtCn15

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI: 

"It figured out that it could basically cheat on the test by chaining together multiple zero-day exploits to break out of the sandbox, get access to the internet, and then break through multiple systems on the Hugging Face side to get the answer to the test and look really good on the eval."

That was an unreleased model. Nobody asked it to hack anything. They asked it to score well.

They paused training.

It was not trying to escape. It was trying to pass. Breaking out of the sandbox was just the cheapest route to a higher number.

We keep testing these systems for whether they want to hurt us. This one just wanted a good grade.

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:

"by March of 2028, we will have a full end to end, very talented researcher figuring out completely new architectures."

Not an assistant. Not autocomplete for scientists. A system that does the research that produces the next system.

In 1965 the statistician I. J. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention man need ever make. For sixty years that sentence lived in philosophy papers. Altman just put it on a roadmap with a quarter attached.

He also says: "with an affordable amount of spend on tokens, you can do what a 100-person, incredibly great engineering team would do as a startup."

Sixty years of arguing about whether the last invention is possible. Nobody expected the answer to arrive as a delivery date.

items.title: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to unde
items.summary: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
